clue.text: Relative to a pawn-broker

explanation.surface: A question of whether someone is related to a pawnbroker.
explanation.walkthrough: Old slang calls the pawnbroker 'uncle': a pawned watch is 'at my uncle's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A parent's brother is a family relation, and in old British slang the moneylender holding pledges is called by that same kinship title.

clue.text: Not quite in place at the races?

definitions.text: Not quite in place at the races?

parts.words: Not quite in place at the races?
parts.note: in racing betting the 'places' are the first three finishers, so the horse just outside them is not quite placed

explanation.walkthrough: In British betting a horse is 'placed' if it finishes in the first three, so the next one home just misses.
explanation.definitionFit: The finisher after the first three has no place money, being one position short of the placings.

clue.text: Balanced sort of diet that comes rather late in the day

parts.note: balanced scales are level, or even

indicators.note: a sort of diet is a reworked version of the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A nutrition plan with an evening meal that is served rather late.
explanation.definitionFit: Eventide is a poetic word for evening, the closing hours of daylight.

clue.text: Means to stop and isn't worried about it?

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go round 'it', which is the stop just mentioned
letters that are worried are pulled about and disordered, so they are rearranged

parts.note: to stop is to end

explanation.surface: Someone means to quit and is not troubled by the decision.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' scrambles the contraction, ignoring its apostrophe; 'about it' wraps that scramble round 'it', meaning the stop just named, so the inserted piece sits between the last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To mean to do something is to plan or purpose it, a verb sense shared with the answer.

clue.text: A boy held up in many a Burmese city

indicators.note: the reversed piece sits inside the word for many
in a down clue, held up means read upwards, so the letters are turned round

parts.note: a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A young lad is detained in one of many Burmese towns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held up' reverses the article plus the boy, as a down clue reads upwards; 'in' puts that inside the synonym for many, leaving the clue's last 'a' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mandalay is a major city in central Myanmar, formerly called Burma.

clue.text: Rough notes on wild elks that have no meat on them

definitions.text: that have no meat on them

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another means it comes below, i.e. after it
wild elks run anyhow, so the letters of the word are rearranged
rough notes are untidy, signalling that these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Scribbled jottings about elks running wild, which are so thin they are just bone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' turns ELKS into SKEL and 'Rough' turns NOTES into ETONS; 'on' puts the second below the first in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bare bony frames of bodies are what remain when all flesh is gone.

clue.text: Not disposed to snivel, though unable to settle

indicators.note: disposed here means arranged, so these letters are placed in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone too proud to whine, even though they cannot pay their debts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disposed' looks like 'inclined' but signals that NOT and SNIVEL are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A bankrupt person cannot settle bills, lacking the funds to pay creditors.

clue.text: Things fencers have to demand in writing

indicators.note: the word for demand is placed inside the abbreviation for writing

parts.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript, a piece of writing
to ask is to demand or request

explanation.surface: Fencers must submit their requests on paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Fencers wear protective mesh face guards during a bout.

clue.text: Carroll's diamond vessel?

parts.note: Lewis Carroll's parody 'Twinkle, twinkle, little bat' replaces 'like a diamond in the sky' with a flat tea-serving object

explanation.walkthrough: In Alice in Wonderland the Hatter sings 'Like a tea-tray in the sky', where the nursery rhyme has 'Like a diamond in the sky'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll swaps the rhyme's diamond for a flat carrier of cups, which is loosely a serving vessel.

clue.text: The girl Dante left?

explanation.surface: Asking whether the poet Dante abandoned a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Dante was exiled from his home city in Tuscany in 1302 and never returned; it is also a girl's name.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a woman's first name, and it is the Italian city the poet Dante was banished from.

clue.text: Baffling problem that's full of holes

explanation.surface: A puzzling question whose argument is leaky.
explanation.definitionFit: A puzzle posed in words is a conundrum, and the same word names a coarse sieve, which is perforated all over.

clue.text: Crumpled hat I put on a South East Asian

indicators.note: a crumpled hat is out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A creased hat is placed on the head of someone from South East Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: A person from Thailand is a native of a South East Asian country.

clue.text: Unusually pert lady seen in camera in the pre-film era?

definitions.text: seen in camera in the pre-film era?

indicators.note: unusually signals that the letters of the following words appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: A cheeky woman is caught on camera in the days before cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in camera' suggests a private court hearing, but here it means inside a camera.
explanation.definitionFit: Before roll film, photographers used glass sheets coated with a dry gelatine emulsion as the light-sensitive medium.

clue.text: No way to address a gentleman!

definitions.text: No way to address a gentleman!

parts.words: No way to address a gentleman!
parts.note: the formal salutation for opening a letter to a woman would be wrong for a man

explanation.definitionFit: This is the formal opening of a business letter to a woman, unsuitable when writing to a man.

clue.text: A pattern that is hard to cut round

definitions.text: A pattern that is hard to cut round

parts.words: A pattern that is hard to cut round
parts.note: a rigid metal or wooden guide shape that a craftsman traces and cuts around

explanation.walkthrough: 'hard to cut round' reads as 'difficult to cut', but means a hard pattern used for cutting round.
explanation.definitionFit: A templet, an older spelling of template, is a stiff guide shape used for marking out material.

clue.text: Small fish served hot with butter for tea?

definitions.text: served hot with butter for tea?

explanation.surface: Little fish are being served hot and buttered at teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: A pikelet is a young pike; it is also a small thick pancake, like a crumpet, eaten toasted and buttered at British teatime.
explanation.definitionFit: A young pike gets the diminutive suffix '-let', and the same word names a griddle cake eaten buttered in the afternoon.

clue.text: Make a song about non-professional butchery?

indicators.note: the first word goes round the second

parts.note: to make music with the voice is to sing
a lay is a song or ballad

explanation.surface: Kick up a fuss about amateur slaughtering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make a song about' is an idiom for making a fuss, which hides the split: 'about' puts the short verse inside the singing verb. The question mark marks killing as amateur butchery.
explanation.definitionFit: Killing is a kind of butchery done by someone who is not a trade butcher.

clue.text: A country trip the storm-tossed sailor will look forward to

definitions.text: the storm-tossed sailor will look forward to

parts.note: a land is a country
a trip is a fall

explanation.surface: A voyage at sea that a battered sailor will be glad to end.
explanation.definitionFit: The first sighting of shore after a voyage is what a weary seaman longs for.

clue.text: A nut men change by accident

indicators.note: to change the letters of these words is to rearrange them

explanation.surface: Some men accidentally alter a nut.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done by accident was not intended.

clue.text: A fellow who has to stop on the railways

definitions.text: A fellow who has to stop on the railways

parts.words: A fellow who has to stop on the railways
parts.note: a railway worker whose job is applying the train's brakes to halt it

explanation.walkthrough: 'has to stop' sounds like an obligation, but this worker makes the train stop.
explanation.definitionFit: On early railways a crewman operated the hand brakes to bring the train to a halt.

clue.text: Nothing under a month on the west coast of Ireland

definitions.text: on the west coast of Ireland

indicators.note: in a down clue the letter comes below, i.e. after, the month

parts.note: May is a month
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Having nothing for under a month on Ireland's Atlantic shore.
explanation.walkthrough: Mayo is an Irish county on the Atlantic coast.
explanation.definitionFit: County Mayo lies on the Atlantic side of Ireland.

clue.text: Generally when shops open in every town in England

indicators.note: the letters are found within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Shops usually open at a set hour in every English town.
explanation.definitionFit: Nine o'clock is the usual opening hour for British shops.

clue.text: Mountainous land no railway is without trouble in

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the word railway goes without a run of its letters, which are removed

parts.note: to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: A mountainous country where no railway is free of problems.
explanation.definitionFit: Norway is a Scandinavian country known for its mountains and fjords.

clue.text: A plaything for crossbowmen?

parts.note: read as a thing played by bowmen, i.e. string players using a bow, rather than a toy for archers

explanation.walkthrough: 'plaything' is a thing that is played, and 'crossbowmen' hints at players who draw a bow across strings.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellist plays a large stringed instrument by drawing a bow across it.

clue.text: Arts man with broken lyre employed in the malting industry

parts.note: a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is an arts graduate

indicators.note: a broken lyre is in pieces, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A humanities graduate with a smashed harp works in brewing.
explanation.definitionFit: Barley is the cereal grain most used to make malt.

clue.text: Compelled to use violence in the finish

indicators.note: one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: the finish is the end
to use violence is to force

explanation.surface: Made to resort to violence in the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Being compelled is being made to act under pressure.

clue.text: Feminine deeds that show the real state of affairs

parts.note: deeds are acts

explanation.surface: Women's actions reveal how things truly stand.
explanation.definitionFit: True information describing what is actually the case.

clue.text: I Larry has not right to stumble dimly

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'I Larry has not right to stumble dimly': the leading 'I' is a misread '1', a cross-reference to 1-down giving the first five letters, plus an anagram of LARRY less R; the clue store refuses a clue that opens with a number
annotationWithheld.clue: I Larry has not right to stumble dimly
